clinicalPearls: Sinonasal mesenchymal tumour showing perivascular myoid (glomus-like) differentiation; historically termed sinonasal-type haemangiopericytoma.
Classified as a borderline, low-malignant-potential neoplasm rather than a frankly aggressive sarcoma.
Typically presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis, sometimes with a visible polypoid mass.
Activating CTNNB1 mutations are characteristic, producing nuclear beta-catenin accumulation on immunohistochemistry.
Tumour cells express smooth muscle actin and muscle-specific actin; STAT6 is negative, which helps exclude solitary fibrous tumour.
Histology shows a syncytial proliferation of bland spindle to ovoid cells around branching 'staghorn' vessels with prominent perivascular hyalinisation.
Complete surgical excision is usually curative, but incomplete resection predisposes to local recurrence.
Overtly malignant behaviour (marked pleomorphism, brisk mitoses, necrosis, large size, bone invasion) and metastasis are uncommon.
reference.pathophysiology: Glomangiopericytoma is a sinonasal mesenchymal neoplasm arising from perivascular modified smooth muscle cells with glomus-like (myoid) differentiation. It characteristically carries activating mutations in CTNNB1, the gene encoding beta-catenin, resulting in nuclear accumulation of beta-catenin and activation of Wnt signalling that drives proliferation. Macroscopically it forms a soft, red-grey polypoid mass within the nasal cavity. Histologically there is a diffuse, syncytial proliferation of bland, closely packed spindled to ovoid cells surrounding a rich network of thin-walled branching (staghorn) vessels, typically with prominent perivascular hyalinisation. Mitotic activity is generally low and necrosis uncommon; features that predict more aggressive behaviour include large size, marked nuclear pleomorphism, brisk mitotic activity, necrosis and bone invasion.
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy with direct visualisation of the mass
CT of the sinuses to define extent and bony involvement
MRI for soft-tissue characterisation and orbital or intracranial extension
Immunohistochemistry (smooth muscle actin, nuclear beta-catenin, STAT6-negative, variable CD34)
Pre-operative angiography with consideration of embolisation for highly vascular lesions
redFlags: Bone destruction or rapid growth suggesting malignant behaviour
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, with a high cure rate after complete surgical excision. Local recurrence occurs in a minority, particularly after incomplete resection, whereas overtly malignant behaviour with metastasis is uncommon.
pitfalls: Confusing it with solitary fibrous tumour; STAT6 immunostaining resolves the distinction.
Mislabelling it as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, particularly in younger patients.
Incomplete excision predisposing to local recurrence.
Equating it with soft-tissue haemangiopericytoma, which has different biology and behaviour.
